title: Spreading a generic fibre component to a clopen piece
statement: Let $g:P\to T$ be a finite type morphism of schemes (locally of finite type and quasi-compact, as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]). Let $y\in T$ and $x\in P$ satisfy $g(x)=y$. There exist an ambient open $V\subseteq T$ with $y\in V$ and a subset $A\subseteq P$ whose trace on $g^{-1}(V\cap\overline{\{y\}})$ is clopen for the subspace topology, and such that $g^{-1}(\{y\})\cap A$ is exactly the connected component of $x$ in the fibre $g^{-1}(\{y\})$. No assertion is made about connectedness of fibres over points other than $y$.

source.place: Tag 055N, integral-base proof through clopenness of the closure; Tags 054Y and 054W

proof.text: give the closure of y its reduced closed subscheme structure and base change g. This is an integral base with generic point y. The generic fibre is finite type over a field, hence noetherian, so the component of x and its complement are clopen. Take their closures in the base-changed total space. Their generic fibres are the original subsets. Tag 054Y shrinks the base so the two closures cover the total space. Their intersection has empty generic fibre; Tag 054W shrinks again so the intersection is empty. Each closure is now clopen, and its trace on the generic fibre is unchanged. The base change by the reduced closed immersion is a homeomorphism onto the inverse image of the closure of y. Represent the open of that closure by an ambient open V, and represent the chosen closure by a subset A of P under this homeomorphism. The generic point belongs to V, and the trace of A on its fibre is exactly the component of x. Empty complements cause no problem: the same closure argument applies.

lean.statement:
theorem exists_open_generic_fibre_component_spread {P T : Scheme.{u}} (g : P ⟶ T)
    [LocallyOfFiniteType g] [QuasiCompact g] (y : T) (x : P) (hx : g x = y) :
    ∃ (V : Set T) (A : Set P), IsOpen V ∧ y ∈ V ∧
      IsClopen {q : g ⁻¹' (V ∩ closure {y}) | (q : P) ∈ A} ∧
      g ⁻¹' {y} ∩ A = connectedComponentIn (g ⁻¹' {y}) x
